title: Perbandingan Word2Vec dan N-Gram pada Klasifikasi Sentimen Gaji Guru Honorer Mengggunakan Support Vector Machine
abstract: Komentar pengguna Instagram dapat dimanfaatkan untuk menggambarkan persepsi masyarakat terhadap berbagai isu sosial, termasuk kesejahteraan guru honorer. Penelitian ini mengevaluasi pengaruh dua pendekatan representasi teks, yaitu Word2Vec dan N-Gram berbasis TF-IDF, terhadap performa klasifikasi sentimen menggunakan algoritma Support Vector Machine (SVM). Dataset komentar Instagram diproses melalui tahapan pembersihan teks dan pelabelan sentimen sebelum dilakukan penyeimbangan kelas menggunakan Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE). Representasi teks yang diuji meliputi Word2Vec CBOW, Word2Vec Skip-Gram, TF-IDF Unigram, Bigram, dan Trigram. Evaluasi dilakukan menggunakan Stratified 5-Fold Cross Validation dengan kernel Linear, Polynomial, Radial Basis Function (RBF), dan Sigmoid. Hasil eksperimen menunjukkan bahwa TF-IDF Unigram memberikan kinerja terbaik dengan akurasi 94,87%, sedangkan Word2Vec CBOW, TF-IDF Bigram, Word2Vec Skip-Gram, dan TF-IDF Trigram masing-masing memperoleh akurasi 87,04%, 86,35%, 85,78%, dan 77,22%. Selain mencapai akurasi tertinggi, TF-IDF Unigram juga menghasilkan nilai precision, recall, dan F1-score sebesar 95%. Temuan ini menunjukkan bahwa representasi berbasis kata tunggal dengan pembobotan TF-IDF lebih efektif dalam mengidentifikasi sentimen komentar Instagram dibandingkan pendekatan Word2Vec pada dataset yang digunakan.Kata Kunci: N-Gram ; Support Vector Machine; TF-IDF; Word2Vec; analisis sentimen

title: HUMAN-CENTERED EXPLAINABLE AI FOR ADAPTIVE RESOURCE ALLOCATION AND DECISION GOVERNANCE IN SERVICE ORGANIZATIONS
abstract: Service organizations increasingly employ artificial intelligence and predictive analytics to allocate financial, technological, workforce, and operational resources. Although algorithmic systems can process complex organizational data, purely prediction-driven approaches may generate recommendations that are difficult for managers to interpret, validate, or reconcile with organizational constraints. These limitations become particularly important in healthcare and other information-intensive service environments where resource allocation decisions interact with workforce capacity, digital workflows, privacy requirements, project priorities, and service quality objectives. This study proposes a human centered explainable artificial intelligence framework for adaptive resource allocation and decision governance. The framework integrates predictive modeling, multi objective optimization, and explainability mechanisms within a structured decision support architecture. Rather than optimizing a single performance measure, the proposed approach considers multiple objectives including operational efficiency, resource utilization, service responsiveness, workforce capacity, fairness, and decision transparency. A human-in-the-loop governance mechanism allows decision-makers to review explanations, modify organizational constraints, and evaluate alternative allocation scenarios before recommendations are implemented. Because real organizational data are not used in the present study, the framework is evaluated using synthetically generated operational environments representing variations in demand, workforce availability, resource limitations, project priorities, and unexpected disruptions. Scenario and sensitivity analyses can then examine how resource allocation recommendations change under alternative organizational conditions. The principal contribution is an integrated analytical architecture in which optimization and explainability operate as complementary components of organizational decision making. The proposed framework can provide a foundation for transparent resource allocation systems applicable to healthcare, professional services, digital enterprises, and other service-oriented organizations seeking to improve efficiency and resilience while retaining managerial oversight.

title: Supplemental generative AI tutoring improves financial modeling scores in a two class quasi experimental study
abstract: This study examined the association between supplemental generative artificial intelligence (AI) tutoring and score improvement in financial modeling education using a two-class quasi-experimental design. Eighty-eight undergraduate students enrolled in two scheduled sections of a financial modeling course at a university in China were assigned to an experimental group (EG, $$n = 45$$ ) that received traditional teaching plus supplemental generative AI tutoring, or to a control group (CG, $$n = 43$$ ) that received traditional teaching only. The primary analysis was an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) on post-test scores controlling for pre-test scores, complemented by prespecified sensitivity analyses on gain scores. Both groups improved significantly from pre-test to post-test. The EG obtained significantly higher adjusted post-test scores than the CG, with an adjusted mean difference of 2.13 points (95% CI [0.58, 3.68]) and a medium standardized between-group difference in gain scores (Cohen’s $$d = 0.57$$ , 95% CI [0.15, 1.02]). A Group $$\times$$ Pre-test interaction was not statistically significant and is interpreted as a hypothesis-generating signal only. No significant between-group difference in post-test learning engagement was observed. These findings indicate that supplemental generative AI tutoring was associated with greater score improvement; however, the two-class quasi-experimental design, the confounding of tutoring access with additional time on task, and the single-institution sample limit causal generalizations. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: Global-in-time Spectral Duhamel-Picard Method for Post-Exposure Bake Simulation and Physics-Informed Neural Operators for EUV Lithography
abstract: We present a global-in-time spectral Duhamel-Picard method with polynomial expansions for post-exposure bake (PEB) simulation. The coupled acid-quencher reaction-diffusion equations are reformulated as nonlinear Volterra integral equations using the Duhamel principle. Full trajectories are represented by finite polynomial expansions, with temporal coefficient fields determined over the bake interval by Anderson-accelerated Picard iteration, thereby avoiding sequential time marching. In 3-D PEB simulations, we employ Chebyshev and Legendre temporal bases while evaluating the Duhamel integrals using the corresponding Gaussian quadrature rules. We demonstrate that the proposed method simulates a large domain of $1200\times1200\times100$ voxels on the order of one minute. The representation is further incorporated into a physics-informed neural operator (PINO) with a mixed-transform variant of a factorized Fourier neural operator, which is trained without precomputed solution trajectories. Together, the integral formulation and its PINO extension enable accelerated, time-marching-free prediction of concentration fields at arbitrary times within the bake interval.

title: Combining Post-Quantum Cryptography and Quantum Key Distribution: Taxonomy, Constructions, Proofs, Standards, Deployments and Open Problems
abstract: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) address the quantum threat from opposite directions: PQC replaces vulnerable public-key algorithms with schemes believed to resist quantum cryptanalysis, while QKD derives keys whose secrecy rests on physical assumptions rather than computational ones. Because each approach has a distinct failure mode, a growing body of work combines them so that a session key remains secure if either component holds. We first establish the deployed baseline, hybrid classical-plus-PQC key exchange, against which QKD-augmented designs must be judged. We then propose a taxonomy of hybrid PQC-QKD designs along eight dimensions (integration layer, combiner construction, authentication scope and source, QKD topology, trusted entities, key-delivery interface, classical component, and evidence type), and use it to compare published protocols, including Muckle and its successors, MACsec and TLS integrations, and IKEv2 mechanisms standardised in RFCs 8784, 9370, and 9867. We examine key-combiner constructions in light of the KEM-combiner literature and of NIST, ETSI, and ITU-T guidance, and map the security arguments for hybrid PQC-QKD protocols onto a common grid of security model, assumptions, permitted compromise, established guarantee, and limitations. We synthesise deployment evidence from metropolitan and national QKD networks, distinguishing the few testbeds that have run PQC in the key path from pure-QKD deployments, and summarise the standards and policy landscape, including the positions of national security agencies that recommend against relying on QKD alone. We close with open problems: authentication of the QKD classical channel, shared-infrastructure threat models, device certification versus formal proofs, formal verification of hybrid handshakes, and the lack of peer-reviewed deployment economics.

title: Concealed Handgun Detection using WiFi Signals
abstract: While conventional camera-based surveillance systems and metal detectors can provide a sufficient level of security when used appropriately, they have fundamental limitations that reduce their applicability. Camera-based systems are unable to detect occluded or concealed threats and metal detectors require each person to enter through a narrow opening one at a time, leading to congestion issues and limited use in large crowds. A WiFi-based security system has the potential to be a complementary modality that is able to handle occlusions or concealment and is not hindered by strict spatial configurations. In this paper, we propose use Channel State Information estimated from WiFi-signals to detect concealed handguns. To this end we collect a dataset of aligned WiFi signals and RGB images that we call the WiFire dataset. We also propose a deep learning model called WiFireNet tailored to detect concealed handguns in WiFi signals using vision-based supervision signals. Our results show that concealed handgun detection is possible in WiFi and has promise as a complementary modality to surveillance cameras and metal detectors. We release the dataset, model and code to facilitate the further research into WiFi-based handgun detection.

title: Two For The Price Of One: Curvature-Aware Pruning Preserves Influence Functions Too
abstract: Post-training pruning enables efficient deployment, but conventional methods do not explicitly preserve internal-gradient alignment between sparse and dense models. We study novel connections between downstream performance of compressed models and the ability to retain gradient information via influence-function preservation. Central to this connection is a curvature-aware objective that accounts for both layer activations and backpropagated gradients. Despite its promise, this objective remains underexplored in pruning due to a lack of efficient solvers. We introduce $\texttt{CACTUS}$, a novel ADMM-based optimizer supporting both pruning and sparse-plus-low-rank decompositions of pre-trained weights. Compared to LLM-Surgeon which targets the same objective, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ can achieve over an order-of-magnitude speedup. At $50\%$ pruning of Qwen3-4B, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ reduces the C4 perplexity gap to the dense model by $45\%$, improves compressed-to-dense per-sample gradient cosine similarity on WikiText-2 from $0.670$ to $0.755$, and runs over $28\times$ faster than LLM-Surgeon on substantially weaker hardware. By preserving influence functions, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ supports effective data selection. On Llama-3.2-3B, fine-tuning a fresh dense model on the $5\%$ of data selected by $\texttt{CACTUS}$ achieves $49.44\%$ accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard, compared with $47.22\%$ using ALPS and $49.54\%$ using dense-model selection. Finally, integrating $\texttt{CACTUS}$ with LoGRA, a recent gradient-projection strategy, on Qwen3-4B with MLP layers pruned to 2:4 sparsity and a rank-64 correction retains a $0.711$ cosine alignment with dense LoGRA-projected C4 gradients.

On Llama-3.2-3B, fine-tuning a fresh dense model on the $5\%$ of data selected by $\texttt{CACTUS}$ achieves $49.44\%$ accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard, compared with $47.22\%$ using ALPS and $49.54\%$ using dense-model selection. title: Methods for Automated Equivalence Checking of Quantum Error-Correction Codes
abstract: Quantum error-correction code and circuit construction is an active field of research, motivating automated methods for identifying equivalent designs. We develop and evaluate automated strategies for deciding whether two descriptions of quantum error-correction codes are equivalent under specified transformations. We formalize permutation equivalence for stabilizer and CSS codes and local-Clifford equivalence for stabilizer codes within a unified framework that separates physical from representation freedom. We develop three decision strategies (group-action search, isomorphism-based methods, and constraint solving), together with invariants and signatures for preprocessing. The empirical evaluation shows that no paradigm dominates across equivalence notions, code families, and parameter ranges. We therefore combine their complementary strengths in input-dependent hybrid checkers following a staged Refute-Refine-Decide architecture. Mean hybrid runtimes remain below 10 s for most evaluated structured-code cases with $n \leq 37$; for inequivalent code instances with $n=144$, they are about 310 s for permutation and 16 s for local-Clifford equivalence.

title: Surface Reconstruction from Range Scans Under Visibility Constraints
abstract: Surface reconstruction from range scans is challenging in the presence of noise and outliers, as fidelity to observations must be balanced against sensitivity to measurement errors. Yet, most neural approaches discard the sensor positions and corresponding visibility information, compensating for this loss with geometric priors or regularization terms. We instead formulate surface reconstruction as robust regression of the predicted first surface intersection along each acquisition ray against its measured depth, which penalizes predicted surface intersections within the segment between the sensor and the observed point. We represent the surface as the zero set of a 1-Lipschitz multi-layer perceptron, allowing the use of linearly convergent sphere tracing to compute the first hit, and use a robust Huber loss for regression. Our formulation requires neither oriented normals, sampled off-surface points, nor an eikonal loss. Comparisons with the state of the art on synthetic and real data with varying levels of noise and outlier contamination demonstrate competitive performance on clean data and much improved fidelity and robustness under even moderate corruption. Our analysis further confirms a trade-off between fidelity and robustness: greater fitting capacity improves data fidelity in the clean case but increases sensitivity to the measurement errors inherent in real acquisitions, with a sweet spot typically emerging at intermediate capacity.

title: Local Leakage Resilience of Shamir Secret Sharing: Below Half Threshold Rate
abstract: We study the local leakage resilience of Shamir secret sharing, where an adversary leaks a bounded number of bits from every share. For $n$ parties and reconstruction threshold $k$ over a prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $p>n$, we prove the following. (1) There is an absolute constant $c_{\mathrm{bh}}<1/2$ such that, for $k\ge c_{\mathrm{bh}}n$, Shamir sharing is resilient to arbitrary one-bit leakage from every share. The best previous threshold was $0.668n$. (2) For every fixed $0<δ<1/2$ and $k\ge(1/2+δ)n$, Shamir sharing is resilient to $\left\lfloor\fracδ{24}\log_2 n\right\rfloor$ bits of arbitrary local leakage per share. By a recent attack, this number of bits is optimal up to a constant factor depending on $δ$. (3) For every fixed threshold rate $c>0$ and $k\ge cn$, Shamir sharing is resilient to quadratic-residue leakage and to almost all local leakage functions of up to $η_c\log_2 p$ bits, for a constant $η_c>0$. All three results follow from one analytic framework, which we develop for generalized Reed--Solomon codes: local leakage from a uniform codeword is statistically close to the same leakage from independent uniform field elements. The framework expresses the leakage distance as the norm of a function on the leakage outputs. The Efron--Stein decomposition splits this function into orthogonal components indexed by supports of dual codewords. Two tools bound the components: list recovery of the dual code, which is ordinary list decoding for one-bit leakage, and a generalized von Neumann inequality for MDS systems of linear forms that retains linearly many Gowers norms. The first tool gives the result above half, the second gives the constant-rate result, and applying both to different ranges of supports in the same decomposition gives the result below half.

title: A (partial*) graph of relationships between traditional agri-food LCA resources and the wider "Semantic Web"
abstract: A (partial*) graph of relationships between traditional agri-food LCA resources and the wider “Semantic Web:” An aid to a linking proposal for the FOODTURE agrifood database. *Note: many links are missing. If all links were shown, the graph would be unreadable, as such, the graph is meant for illustrative purposes only and should not be taken as a complete guide. The main focus of the links shown is to orient the FOODTURE database in the wider universe of semantic and LCA resources.

title: The Price of Thinking: An Amortization Rule for How Much an AI Should Reason
abstract: An AI system can organize its reasoning in several ways: answer directly, explore and select among alternatives, or first change the representation of the problem. Recent work lets AI systems search over such modes on benchmark tasks, and selects them for accuracy. This note adds the missing economic step. Reasoning has a cost that is paid once, while what it produces (an algorithm, a workflow, a reasoning template) is often used many times. Writing the total cost as a price of thinking times the reasoning cost plus the number of uses times the per-use loss gives a break-even rule between modes. The modes worth keeping in a portfolio lie on a convex frontier that does not depend on the price of thinking. The cost of selecting a mode is itself amortized over the tasks of a given type, which bounds the regress of reasoning about reasoning. A second part treats the allocation of reasoning during a task: the branches of a search are judged on their progression rather than on their level, the limit a branch is heading to is projected by Aitken’s extrapolation, and a branch stops when the gain expected from its next tranche no longer pays for it. Small experiments illustrate both parts. When four modes build a cube solver at equal budget without any prior knowledge of the cube, the least usual mode, representation first, gives the shortest solutions at the lowest cost, while an explicit search tree whose branches are fixed in advance costs four times more for an intermediate result. Allocating the tree’s reasoning by tranches improves on it, and shows why a young branch must be judged on its progression. On the 2 × 2 cube, where every distance is known, the length of a solution splits exactly into the optimum plus the waste of its steps, and choosing the first stage of a nested solution on its net progress removes almost all the waste, at a cost that grows geometrically.

title: Quantifying the Accuracy-Explainability Trade-off in Statistical and Machine Learning Models Across Multiple Clinical Datasets: A Cross-Pathology Validation Framework
abstract: Objective: The rapid digitisation of healthcare has necessitated the development of high-performance predictive models for clinical diagnostics. While traditional statistical frameworks such as Multiple Logistic Regression (MLR) are favoured for their intrinsic interpretability, they often encounter an accuracy ceiling when applied to complex, non-linear clinical data. Conversely, advanced machine learning ensembles such as eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) offer superior classification ability but suffer from the black-box problem. This study aims to quantify the accuracy-explainability trade-off by comparing a transparent baseline against an Explainable AI (XAI)-augmented pipeline across three distinct clinical datasets. Methods: This study employs a multi-cohort comparative framework using the Heart Failure Clinical Records (n = 299), Wisconsin Breast Cancer Diagnostic (n = 569), and Pima Indians Diabetes (n = 768) datasets, representing cardiovascular, oncological, and metabolic diagnostic spaces, respectively. The methodology incorporates a Phase 2 Clinical Assay Development framework with 10-fold stratified cross-validation and Parallelised Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV) as a high-fidelity sensitivity audit. DeLong’s test for correlated ROC curves and the Ramsey RESET test were employed to evaluate the significance of performance and structural misspecification. A 2,000-iteration bootstrap stability audit was executed to verify estimator consistency. Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were applied as a post-hoc audit framework, with reliability verified via an Explanatory Stability Score (S). Results: Model superiority is dictated by a complexity threshold tied to data geometry. In high-dimensional oncological data, XGBoost demonstrated significant superiority over MLR (AUC 0.994 vs. 0.941; p < 0.001), structurally mandated by a massive RESET misspecification (p < 10−52). A LOOCV sensitivity check revealed a statistical tie (p = 0.676), with a bootstrap 95% CI of [−0.0047, 0.0066] that contains zero, positioning MLR as a robust and parsimonious champion when target leakage is controlled. The cardiovascular cohort exhibited a stable tie (95% CI: [−0.0564, 0.0378]), and the metabolic cohort demonstrated clear linear sufficiency (RESET p = 0.112), resulting in significant MLR superiority over XGBoost (p = 0.0006). SHAP stability metrics (S > 0.80) confirmed that audited signatures represent robust biological markers rather than stochastic artefacts. Conclusion: This research establishes that the accuracy-explainability trade-off is not a static penalty but a dynamic threshold dictated by clinical dimensionality and data geometry. By providing a mathematically validated framework incorporating structural diagnostics, bootstrap stability, and SHAP-based explainability, this study demonstrates that diagnostic tools can achieve peak accuracy without sacrificing the transparency required for clinical accountability.

title: Autoencoder-assisted variational Gaussian process mineral prospectivity mapping for the Okiep Copper District, South Africa
abstract: The Okiep Copper District in Namaqualand, South Africa, is a historically important copper province in which mineralisation is hosted mainly by small, irregular Koperberg Suite intrusions and associated structural corridors. This study develops an autoencoder-assisted variational Gaussian process workflow for district-scale Cu mineral prospectivity mapping. Multisource geological, geochemical, geophysical, terrain, spectral, and spatial evidence layers were harmonised on an H3 resolution-10 spatial support, producing 681,385 modelling cells, including 43 cells containing known Cu occurrences. The workflow is framed as positive-versus-background learning: cells without known occurrences were treated as unlabelled background rather than verified barren ground, and VGP outputs were interpreted as relative prospectivity scores rather than calibrated probabilities of undiscovered mineralisation. Autoencoder reconstruction improved rapidly from a coefficient of determination of approximately 0.73 at coding-layer size 5 to approximately 0.84 at coding-layer size 17. Coding-layer sizes 17–29 exceeded the 98% maximum coefficient of determination threshold and were propagated into the VGP ensemble. Across the selected latent spaces, VGP models showed strong internal discrimination, with many trials recording cross-validation scores above 0.96, weighted F1 scores above 0.92, and AUC-ROC values above 0.94. These metrics are used only as internal ranking diagnostics for model discrimination. Ensemble mean prospectivity, ensemble standard deviation, and target-selection frequency identify a coherent eastern to south-eastern prospective tract that overlaps known Cu deposits and defines new ranked target areas. The workflow provides a reproducible target hierarchy for brownfield copper exploration while separating model-related uncertainty from unresolved data-related uncertainty.

title: GreenWAM: A World Foundation Model for Robotics
abstract: A robot needs a world model that predicts how its actions will change the scene and a policy that chooses those actions. Models are usually built and evaluated for only one of these roles, and every robot records its actions in its own format. We ask whether one robot world model can serve both roles across different bodies, and what makes this work. We present GreenWAM, a world foundation model for robotics, together with the recipe that produces it: (1) a shared anatomical action space that describes 20 robot families, from bimanual arms to dexterous humanoids, in common joint coordinates; (2) joint training on these families in visual, action-conditioned and world-action modes; and (3) policies that split an action expert off the generator. As a world model, GreenWAM attains top-tier trajectory, depth and 3D accuracy on WorldArena 1.0, ahead of every world-action model and video generator in our comparison. As a policy, it scores among the top entries of the RoboTwin 2.0 leaderboard, reaches the highest zero-shot LIBERO-plus success among the compared methods and is competitive with dedicated vision-language-action and world-action policies on CALVIN and LIBERO. We further adapt GreenWAM to a real humanoid, where it succeeds more often than policies adapted from π_{0.5} and from Cosmos 3 Edge, and distill it into a single-step policy for real-time control. Controlled experiments yield three findings: robot specialization improves world prediction and control together; an action expert helps when split off at the start of adaptation; and keeping world-model modes during policy adaptation preserves robustness to scene changes.

title: Behavioural self-monitoring for autonomous earth observation agents: The attribute reliability monitor (ARM)
abstract: Language and vision language models can support autonomous systems, but changing operating conditions may compromise the reliability of their semantic outputs. This work introduces the Attribute Reliability Monitor (ARM), a framework that accumulates evidence of suspicion over time to assess individual semantic attributes. ARM accommodates different detectors and temporal monitoring methods, while leaving intervention policies to the consuming system. An initial implementation was evaluated using a specialized vision language model developed for satellite thermal infrared imagery. Monitoring followed a black box approach, using only observable responses without access to internal model states, confidence scores, or external reference answers. Under controlled input degradation, disagreement between responses provided evidence for selective suspension of attributes. The results illustrate how external behavioral monitoring can inform continued use of model outputs, while distinguishing operational suspicion from semantic correctness.

title: A Global View of How LLMs Value Human Time
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as personal assistants; however, little is known about how they capture national-level preferences on a global scale. Given that "time" is a universal and representative concept, we examine LLMs' time preferences by varying only users' country and measuring the compensation LLMs deem appropriate for a 60-minute appointment delay. We then compare LLMs' responses with GDP per capita on Purchasing Power Parity (GDP_PPP), Mean Income, and a literature-based index (Patience Score). Our results across 193 countries and 5 LLMs demonstrate that people's time across the world is evaluated in noticeably different ways among LLMs, as well as varying levels of robustness under prompt variations. LLMs consistently recommend the highest compensation for Europe, but mostly the lowest for Africa. Based on GDP_PPP, LLMs underestimate the value of time for users living in Asia and South America. These findings indicate that geographical patterns are embedded in LLMs and may translate in different treatment in agentic settings.

title: FALLNEST: Dual-Domain Dataset Condensation of Imbalanced IMU Data for Wearable Fall Detection
abstract: Wearable fall detection is hampered by rare fall events, scarce labeled IMU data, and the cost of training deep models on large, imbalanced corpora. Existing methods either rely on hand-crafted features with shallow classifiers, which limits learning from raw signals, or train deep networks on full datasets that require re-sampling to counter class skew and demand substantial data and compute. To address this, we propose a novel Fall detection framework via Normalized-gradient and Embedding matched Synthetic Time-frequency condensation, dubbed FALLNEST, a data-centric approach that distills large, imbalanced IMU datasets into tiny, class-balanced synthetic training sets. Building on dual-domain time-series condensation (CondTSC), FALLNEST introduces a fall-specific 7-channel input with accelerometer vector magnitude, class-balanced K-Means initialization, and normalized gradient matching with gradient clipping, combined with MMD-based embedding alignment and multi-view Fourier-domain augmentation, so that class balance arises from the condensed set itself rather than from re-sampling. We evaluate on SisFall, KFall, and MobiFall using strict subject-wise splits and naturally imbalanced test sets, reporting accuracy, Macro-F1, and PR-AUC over five seeds. A 102K-parameter TinyCNN trained on only 32 to 146 synthetic windows (about only 1% of the training windows) reaches 93.5-95.8% mean accuracy and 0.89-0.98 PR-AUC, with standard deviations of 1.0-1.7% in accuracy, demonstrating the efficacy of our approach.

Building on dual-domain time-series condensation (CondTSC), FALLNEST introduces a fall-specific 7-channel input with accelerometer vector magnitude, class-balanced K-Means initialization, and normalized gradient matching with gradient clipping, combined with MMD-based embedding alignment and multi-view Fourier-domain augmentation, so that class balance arises from the condensed set itself rather than from re-sampling. We evaluate on SisFall, KFall, and MobiFall using strict subject-wise splits and naturally imbalanced test sets, reporting accuracy, Macro-F1, and PR-AUC over five seeds. A 102K-parameter TinyCNN trained on only 32 to 146 synthetic windows (about only 1% of the training windows) reaches 93.5-95.8% mean accuracy and 0.89-0.98 PR-AUC, with standard deviations of 1.0-1.7% in accuracy, demonstrating the efficacy of our approach.

title: SWEPatchTest: Evaluating Software Tests Beyond Reproduction
abstract: Coding agents use generated tests to decide whether a proposed patch satisfies an issue's requirements. A suite that fails on the buggy program and passes after applying the reference patch can still accept an incorrect patch or reject a correct patch. We introduce SWEPATCHTEST, a test-generation benchmark with 619 tasks from SWE-bench Pro, SWE-bench Multilingual, and DeepSWE and 82,579 candidate patches collected from coding-agent trajectories. By replaying each suite on the buggy and patched codebases, \benchmark jointly measures issue reproduction, acceptance of correct patches, and rejection of incorrect patches. Joint Validation Rate (JVR), which requires all three criteria on the same task, exposes failures hidden by single-reference evaluation: the best-performing configuration achieves only 9.21% JVR despite reproducing the reference transition on 59.29% of tasks. We further use validation scores to select and scale demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The resulting training recipe approximately triples JVR and improves downstream repair across three SWE-bench benchmarks. Patch discrimination thus provides both a diagnostic measure of test quality and an execution-based signal for curating agent training data.

title: Autonomous 3D Visual-Thermal Inspection for Utility-Scale Solar Farms
abstract: Utility-scale photovoltaic (PV) inspection is dominated by aerial surveys, which are effective for identifying module-level hot cells but provide limited visibility of critical components located under the array, including connectors, cabling, fasteners and structural elements. These assets are difficult to inspect consistently at scale, and their defects are often spatially small, partially occluded and difficult to localise from isolated images. We present an automated 3D visual-thermal inspection system (Tricorder) for under-panel PV asset inspection. The approach combines LiDAR-inertial Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) with geometrically calibrated RGB and thermal imagery and machine-learning-based object detection and segmentation. Detected assets are associated with the reconstructed 3D environment, allowing visual and thermal observations from multiple viewpoints to be spatially fused and localised. We demonstrate the approach on utility-scale PV data for MC4 connector detection and connection-state recognition, thermal anomaly identification, and detection of structural components including bolts, nuts and torque tubes. The results demonstrate a pathway from image-based inspection toward spatially grounded autonomous inspection, where defects are detected and linked to specific assets and their 3D locations within the solar farm.

title: Convex-Analytic View of Query Selection for Safety Verification of Markov Decision Processes
abstract: Safety verification of a Markov decision process (MDP) asks whether the probabilities of reaching several failure states jointly lie in a convex safe region under every scheduler. Watanabe and Unno (2026) prove safety by refining an outer approximation of the failure probabilities, where each query bounds a nonnegative weighted sum of the probabilities. Their rule selects weights by the largest Euclidean violation. We present a unified framework to measure violation in an explicitly chosen error unit: directions are scored by the support-function gap between the outer approximation and the safe region, normalized by the support function of the unit. We show that the maximal score, when positive, equals the smallest enlargement of the safe region in multiples of that unit that contains the outer approximation. The Euclidean unit recovers the earlier rule; two new rules are generated by the unit cube and the safe region itself. We experimentally evaluate how the choice of measurement rule affects the performance of safety verification for MDPs.

title: Generalised Bit-Vector Abstractions for Formal Verification of Quantum Error-Detection and Entanglement Circuits over $$\{H,X,{\text{C-NOT}}\}$$: CSS Constructions, Soundness, and Mutation-Based Validation
abstract: Abstract Formal verification of quantum circuits becomes increasingly difficult as circuit size increases, since exhaustive reasoning over the underlying Hilbert space is computationally expensive. In previous work [1], we introduced a bit-vector abstraction that separates the tracking of superposition from basis-state behaviour, enabling SMT-based verification of fixed-size error-detection and entanglement circuits constructed from H , X , and C-NOT gates. This paper extends that framework in five directions. First, we generalise the correctness properties to parametrised repetition and concatenated phase-flip codes with up to 101 logical elements. Second, we verify syndrome extraction for CSS codes specified by arbitrary parity-check matrices, including the Steane code, the [[15, 7, 3]] quantum Hamming code, the [[15, 1, 3]] quantum Reed–Muller code, and rotated surface codes with distances up to 101. The verification considers arbitrary error patterns, error detection up to a specified weight, and recovery using a classical decoder. Counterexamples are obtained for errors beyond the correction or detection capability of the respective codes. Third, we characterise the fragment of $$\{H,X,\text {C-NOT}\}$$ circuits for which the abstraction faithfully represents the corresponding Hilbert-space semantics. We prove soundness for this fragment, demonstrate the necessity of the stated conditions through counterexamples, validate the characterisation by differential testing against state-vector simulation, and prove the six lemmas established in the original work. Fourth, we conduct a mutation study using 13 mutation operators and automatically identify equivalent mutants. Within the evaluated fault model, the approach detects all 622 non-equivalent mutants. Fifth, we implement the approach directly using the Z3 API and verify GHZ circuits with up to 262,144 qubits across three topologies on a 16 GB laptop. The evaluation includes repeated measurements and a controlled ablation of the encoding pipeline and solver version. Experiments with random H +C-NOT networks show that verification cost increases steeply with circuit depth when outputs depend on a large number of inputs. The approach is not intended to cover general stabiliser circuits, Y -type stabilisers, fault-tolerant protocols, or physical noise. We identify the extensions required to address these cases.

title: Semanturgie: Abfragen, Datenansichten und nachvollziehbare Ergebnissemantik. Band 2 - Muster, Bindungen, Mehrfachvorkommen und kontrollierte Interpretation
abstract: Semanturgie Band 2: 200 deutsch-englische Arbeitsdefinitionen in zehn Modulen zu Abfragen, Datenansichten und nachvollziehbarer Ergebnissemantik. Alle Einträge sind Bereichsfestlegungen mit konstruiertem Beispiel, Gegenfall und Grenze auf Deutsch. Themen sind Datensätze, RDF-Terme, Muster, Bindungen, Filter, OPTIONAL, Negation, Pfade, Unterabfragen, Aggregation, Projektion, Ordnung und Ergebnisformen. Drei tatsächlich ausgeführte endliche Rechnungen an partiellen Zuordnungen unterscheiden Projektionsduplikate, inneren und äußeren OPTIONAL-Filter sowie MINUS und NOT EXISTS bei disjunktem oder gemeinsamem Bindungsbezug. Der eigene Standardbibliothekscode ist eine begrenzte Algebra-Veranschaulichung, kein SPARQL-Parser, Engine-Test oder Benchmark. Quellenkontexte, tatsächliche Lesetiefe und Erratagrenzen sind ausgewiesen. Keine neue allgemeine Entdeckung, historische Weltpriorität, anerkannte Disziplingründung, Normkonformität, unabhängige Fachbegutachtung, anwaltliche Freigabe oder empirisch gemessene Wirkung des Vokabulars. Volume2 contains 200 paired German-English scoped working definitions on queries, data views and traceable result semantics. Supporting examples, counterexamples and boundaries are in German. Three executed finite mapping calculations distinguish projection duplicates, inner versus outer optional filtering, and MINUS versus NOT EXISTS with disjoint or shared bindings. The original standard-library code is a bounded algebra illustration rather than a SPARQL parser, engine conformance test or runtime benchmark. The named language basis is SPARQL 1.1 of 21 March 2013 with explicit errata limitations. No historical worldwide priority, established discipline, standards conformity, independent peer review, professional legal clearance or empirical vocabulary effectiveness is claimed. Six public files: PDF, TXT, definitions JSON, references JSON, original Python and computed result JSON. PDF and TXT present the same text. CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 applies only to appropriately available rights;cited sources retain their rights. This licence does not generally authorize distribution of adapted versions. No confidential data or personal assessment applications are included.

title: Compressing student history in mathematics knowledge tracing
abstract: This paper investigates how complicated a representation of a student’s past performance has to be to predict what the student will do next. The data used were 1,927,265 mathematics responses from 8,996 Finnish students. Evaluation was conducted on students entirely excluded from model fitting. Predictions based on item identity alone achieved an AUC of .8362. Adding one dynamically updated measure of recent performance raised AUC to .8669. This simple learner state recovered 93.5% of the AUC improvement between the item-only baseline and a query-conditioned transformer (.8690). Increasing the explicit learner state to 50 dimensions raised this proportion to 97.1%, while a 128-dimensional transformer using a common summary of student history achieved an AUC of .8687. The same ordering was observed for log loss, although differences among the richer models were somewhat larger. Thus knowing a student’s recent performance relative to item difficulty captured most of the improvement obtainable from more complex representations of the response sequence.

title: A Novel Data-Driven Approach Integrating DGCN and TILDE-Q for Ultra-Short-Term Photovoltaic Power Forecasting
abstract: Accurate ultra-short-term photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting is essential for the reliable operation and energy management of PV systems. However, rapid irradiance variations and complex meteorological conditions result in highly intermittent, nonlinear, and nonstationary PV power generation. Existing forecasting methods generally focus on temporal dependencies but provide limited representation of the dynamic relationships among meteorological variables and PV power. Moreover, conventional point-wise loss functions do not explicitly preserve the temporal shape of multi-step forecasts. To address these limitations, this study proposes a forecasting framework integrating a dynamic graph convolutional network (DGCN), long short-term memory (LSTM), and the transformation-invariant loss function with distance equilibrium (TILDE-Q). Meteorological variables and historical PV power are represented as graph nodes, and DGCN dynamically learns their sample-specific dependencies. LSTM captures temporal evolution patterns, while TILDE-Q constrains amplitude, phase, and scaling variations to improve trajectory consistency. The proposed method was evaluated on two independent operational PV datasets under 1-, 4-, 8-, and 16-step forecasting horizons, corresponding to 15 min, 1 h, 2 h, and 4 h ahead, respectively. DGCN-LSTM achieved the lowest RMSE and highest R2 across all forecasting horizons on both datasets. Compared with the MAE training objective, TILDE-Q reduced RMSE and MAE by up to 15.35% and 25.90%, respectively, and consistently outperformed DILATE. These results demonstrate that combining dynamic variable-dependency modeling with shape-aware optimization can effectively improve the accuracy and trajectory consistency of multi-step PV power forecasts.

title: From Fourier Amplitudes to Persistence Images for Impact-Echo Defect Detection
abstract: Impact-echo testing is a nondestructive testing method used to detect internal defects in concrete structures. However, boundary reflections, structured interference, and measurement noise can produce complex Fourier amplitude spectra, making defect classification difficult. We constructed a two-dimensional frequency--amplitude persistence image (FA-PI) from the Fourier amplitude spectrum. Using a fixed parameterization of exact multi-parameter persistent homology, each retained Fourier component is represented with frequency-bin location as one coordinate and amplitude as the other, and Gaussian kernels are then applied in this two-dimensional space. This construction has a direct analytical connection to the corresponding one-dimensional Gaussian-smoothed Fourier amplitude spectrum. FA-PI was evaluated on an experimental backfill-void dataset and a public bridge-deck impact-echo dataset, and compared with raw and Gaussian-smoothed Fourier amplitude spectra using a linear classifier with a Softmax output and identical signal-level data splits. The evaluation included original signals and signals corrupted by Gaussian noise, sinusoidal interference, or mixed noise, with matching noise types and signal-to-noise ratios during training, validation, and testing. Performance was assessed using accuracy and macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score. Across the two datasets, FA-PI consistently outperformed the raw and Gaussian-smoothed Fourier baselines in the noisy-condition summaries. These findings indicate that representing Fourier spectral components in a two-dimensional frequency--amplitude space can improve impact-echo defect classification beyond frequency-axis smoothing alone.

title: Approximating Optimal Policies in Heterogeneous Asynchronous Multi-player Bandits
abstract: Motivated by applications to cognitive radio networks, multi-player multi-armed bandits (MMAB) have attracted considerable attention in recent years. The asynchronous variant, in which players are active only at a fraction of timesteps, better reflects real-world decentralized networks, where devices are not permanently active. Despite its practical relevance, this setting remains relatively understudied. Existing work on asynchronous MMAB has focused on homogeneous players, who share the same activation probability, a setting in which the optimal centralized allocation can be easily characterized. In contrast, efficiently computing the optimal allocation in the heterogeneous setting, where players have different activation probabilities, has remained an open problem. In this work, we investigate this problem and first establish its NP-hardness. We then turn to the greedy algorithm, which runs in polynomial time, and prove that it achieves a $\frac{1}{e}$-approximation of the optimal allocation. Furthermore, when players are processed in decreasing order of their activation probabilities, the approximation guarantee improves to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}$. Overall, our results establish the greedy algorithm as an efficient approximation to the optimal allocation, providing a practical oracle baseline for the design of online algorithms for heterogeneous asynchronous multi-player bandits.

title: Optimal Online Regret for Context-Lumpable Bandits
abstract: We study stochastic contextual bandits with an unknown context-lumpable structure. The $S$ contexts are partitioned into $r$ blocks, and every arm has the same mean reward across contexts in the same block. Under arbitrary context distributions and without separation assumptions, we design an algorithm with expected regret $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{r(S+K)T})$, matching the lower bound of Lee et al. (2023) up to logarithmic factors and improving their previous upper bound by a factor of $r$. The algorithm operates over dyadic accuracy levels, using a baseline policy and confidence-based early stopping to control exploration. It then performs cross-context elimination: since rewards are identical within a block, one selected arm eliminates all surviving records from that block, requiring at most $r$ selections at each level. Multi-scale exploration assigns finer accuracies to frequent blocks and coarser accuracies to rare blocks, yielding a near-optimal arm for every block while keeping the weighted policy error small.

title: Development and experimental implementation of noise characterisation techniques on a superconducting quantum processor
abstract: Noise characterisation not only enables error mitigation but also provides valuable information about the intrinsic performance of a quantum device, identifying dominant error contributions and bounding noise stability well beyond the aggregated calibration data. Deploying such methods on a specific hardware topology must combine efficiency and accuracy, assess noise stability, and validate the reconstructed noise model. Here we develop and implement these methods on a superconducting processor with square-lattice topology. First, we revise the cycle-benchmarking protocol and reduce the bias arising from unlearnable degrees of freedom via a regularised cost function. Second, we extend a previously developed tensor-network tomography method to match the device layout and show how its accuracy can be improved by repeated layer execution. Both methods allow approximate sublayer noise models to be extracted from parent ones. Using noise characterisation as a tool, we map the noise structure, track drift, and validate the adequacy of the learnt noise models against experimentally observed noisy estimations in benchmark physical and chemistry circuits. These results inform further improvements in the underlying technology and provide estimates of the size of noise-mitigated circuits that the device can support.

Using noise characterisation as a tool, we map the noise structure, track drift, and validate the adequacy of the learnt noise models against experimentally observed noisy estimations in benchmark physical and chemistry circuits. These results inform further improvements in the underlying technology and provide estimates of the size of noise-mitigated circuits that the device can support.

title: The Protective Power of AI Empathy During Service Failures
abstract: AI-based voice assistants (VAs) are increasingly deployed in digital ecosystems, yet service interaction failures remain common and trigger customer dissatisfaction and verbal aggression. In this paper, we investigate whether AI-expressed empathy serves as a relational buffer against service interaction failures across three online experiments (N = 1,336), including two vignette studies varying failure severity and failure type, and a real-time voice-interaction study. We find that AI empathy has a protective effect that emerges when a failure occurs (Study 1), appears to operate primarily through a relational rather than a substantive channel (Study 2), and replicates with a larger effect size in real voice interactions (Study 3). Convergent evidence from text sentiment and vocal-prosody analyses corroborates the self-report effects. Across all three studies, we replicate a serial mediation effect whereby perceived AI empathy enhances customer outcomes through increased mind perception and social presence. This work contributes to emerging theories of AI empathy by showing that its primary function is not to improve performance broadly, but to buffer the relational consequences of failures in high-stakes service encounters.

title: Implementation Methods and Effects of Sephora AI Marketing
abstract: Nowadays, using AI technology to improve efficiency is one of the most important research subjects. Researchers found that Sephora use AI and AR technology to improve the efficiency of shopping. However, the reason behind efficiency improvements and their broader implication is not been unified. Therefore, this study collects data, including sales growth and so on, and compare it with initial data to examine how the adoption of these technologies enhancing Sephora's operational efficiency. According to the survey, AI technology has as well as enhanced sales efficiency and the experience of consumers transformed the structure of rights and the relationship between AI and consumers. These positive impacts demonstrate that Sephora must continue to use these technologies and refine them further. Besides, these advanced technologies may lead to data privacy leakage and declining consumer trust issues as well. Therefore, solving these issues has also become part of Sephora's efforts to refine these technologies.

title: It Is Not the Phrase; It Is the Expectation: Understanding User Perceptions of Contrastive Negation in AI-Generated Responses
abstract: Recognizable AI writing habits attract public criticism, but their implications for designing conversational interfaces remain unclear. We examine Contrastive Negation (``not X, but Y'') as a case. Two online experiments ($N = 242$), informed by formative interviews and material validation, distinguished response form, negated content, and interlocutor expectations. The construction showed no consistent evaluative or behavioral penalty and slightly increased anthropomorphism. Unexpectable negations increased autonomy threat only under human expectation; compatibility reduced it under AI disclosure. The same supportive replies were received differently across frames: their mood advantage under AI disclosure disappeared under human expectation. Within the human-expected frame, inferred AI authorship accompanied poorer evaluations. Together, the findings distinguish AI recognizability from response quality and acceptance, and motivate grounding attributed user positions and aligning language with interface-created expectations.

title: Causal AI and Structural Causal Models in Foundation Systems: Counterfactual Reasoning, Invariant Representation Learning, and Out-of-Distribution Robustness
abstract: Abstract—Contemporary foundation models—encompassing large language models (LLMs) and vision-language transformers—achieve state-of-the-art predictive performance by identifying complex statistical correlations across massive training distributions. However, standard empirical risk minimization (ERM) operates fundamentally at the lowest rung of Pearl's Causal Hierarchy: the observational level (associational correlation). Consequently, state-of-the-art deep networks suffer from critical failure modes in safety-critical deployments: spurious correlations, algorithmic bias, catastrophic out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization failure under covariate shift, and an intrinsic inability to compute counterfactual queries ('what would have occurred had treatment X been altered?'). Causal Artificial Intelligence (Causal AI) provides the mathematical foundations to bridge associative deep learning with interventional and counterfactual reasoning through Structural Causal Models (SCMs), do-calculus, and invariant representation learning. This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Causal AI integrated into modern foundation models. We formalize Pearl's structural causal framework, establish the mathematical bounds of Invariant Causal Prediction (ICP) and Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM), and derive differentiable score-based directed acyclic graph (DAG) discovery using continuous algebraic constraints (NOTEARS). Furthermore, we construct an enterprise benchmarking testbed across three high-stakes domain corpora: clinical biomedical counterfactual trial synthesis, algorithmic credit fairness under confounders, and visual out-of-distribution robustness under adversarial domain perturbations. Our empirical results demonstrate that incorporating structural causal regularization into transformer representations improves OOD generalization accuracy by 34.6% over standard empirical risk minimization while reducing spurious attribute reliance by 72.8%. Concurrently, interventional do-calculus routing suppresses counterfactual hallucinations in clinical decision support from 28.4% down to 4.2%. Finally, we formulate open research directions in causal representation learning from high-dimensional pixels, automated unobserved confounder discovery, and causal safety alignment for autonomous foundation agents. Index Terms—Causal AI, Structural Causal Models (SCMs), Counterfactual Reasoning, Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM), Pearl's Causal Hierarchy, Do-Calculus, Causal Discovery, Out-of-Distribution Robustness.

title: Android application for multilingual hate speech detection: using XLM-RoBERTa and ONNX optimized
abstract: Aims: Social media and digital platforms face increasing challenges in dealing with multilingual abusive content, which calls for the development of effective solutions for the automatic detection of hate speech. This research presents a practical system for monitoring hate speech in three languages (Arabic, Turkish, and English) based on the improved XLM-RoBERTa model, while exploring ensemble techniques as a baseline for comparison. Methods: FrancophonIA data, consisting of 220,000 texts across the three languages, was used after processing. Baseline models were developed combining Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, and Random Forest using soft voting with TF-IDF feature extraction. The main model was based on XLM-RoBERTa with GPU-accelerated training and an early stop strategy to improve efficiency. The final models were converted to ONNX for compatibility, and a mobile application was created for Android application. Results: The baseline model achieved a macro F1-score of 0.5827, outperforming the individual classifiers. In contrast, the optimized XLM-RoBERTa achieved a substantial improvement of 72.3% accuracy and an macro F1-score of 0.7079 across different languages. Optimization via ONNX enabled efficient real-time inference in both the API and the mobile application. Conclusion: The research proves the feasibility of employing transformer-based multilingual models in building practical content monitoring systems, with the potential for actual deployment on mobile devices to achieve real-time monitoring of hate speech in real-world environments.

title: The Smart Buildings Challenge: Learning Foundation Models for Real-World Optimization at Scale
abstract: Buildings cause nearly 40\% of carbon emissions in the US. Of total building emissions, HVAC systems are responsible for approximately 40-60\% and account for 15\% of global energy consumption. Despite advances in artificial intelligence, most buildings still operate as inefficiently as they did decades ago. Building optimization, perhaps more so than any other optimization problem, has enormous potential for Machine Learning (ML) driven impact on climate change, in both the short and long term. One of the biggest obstacles for building optimization is the lack of policy transfer. Most building control systems, whether simulation or learning based, don't generalize: they only work well for the building they were developed for, but not for other buildings. To solve this problem, we propose a challenge for the development of building foundation models that easily adapt to new buildings with minimal configuration and thereby enable building optimization to scale across the globe. Participants will build control policies on a set of simulated buildings, and have their policies evaluated on an unseen set of buildings. The buildings vary in size, layout, weather, material properties, and HVAC system. Successful outcomes from this initiative promise a massive leap forward in global sustainability efforts and demonstrate the great potential of ML to combat climate change.

title: Saliency-Guided Replay for Continual Learning in Deep Spiking Neural Networks
abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are promising for energy-efficient neuromorphic computing, but they still suffer from catastrophic forgetting when learning tasks sequentially. This work investigates the integration of Experience Packing and Replay (EPR) as a memory-efficient continual learning strategy for deep SNNs under low-latency constraints. The proposed framework combines Batch Normalization Through Time stabilized VGG9 SNNs with Spike Activation Maps (SAM), which provide forward-only explanations based on spike activity. These explanations are temporally aggregated into spatial attention maps and used to select the most informative image patches for replay, instead of storing full images. Experiments on Split CIFAR10 and Split CIFAR100 show that SAM-guided EPR improves the accuracy-memory trade-off under tight memory budgets, and remains competitive while requiring substantially less storage.

title: Gaussian Process Bandits for AI System Optimization with Selectively Verified Feedback
abstract: Gaussian process bandits exploit similarities among configurations to optimize prompts, retrieval systems, and agent workflows. In these applications, however, inexpensive model-based evaluations can disagree with trusted task outcomes. We study selective verification when an action is chosen before a diagnostic is observed and trusted feedback is informative on an unknown set of diagnostic states. A finite reliability class and a finite RKHS signal dictionary describe these two sources of uncertainty. We construct a fixed audit design that combines reliability coverage with reward separation and establish a finite-time regret bound that accounts for a hard audit budget and the rounds needed to obtain informative observations. A safe adaptive extension mixes this robust design with predictable Chernoff allocations while preserving a uniform identification floor and exact expected acquisition-cost accounting. For signed-coordinate kernels, structured and diffuse reliability classes require different audit scales despite sharing the same reward geometry. Synthetic experiments distinguish these certified designs from an adaptive posterior heuristic and GP controls. Safe adaptive allocation reduces aggregate regret relative to the fixed design under the exact dictionary, but its finite-budget error certificate is numerically loose. Conditional-feedback errors can remove the heuristic's advantage and target perturbations can reverse it. Separate AI-task replays assess feedback correction and fitted-dictionary policies without establishing end-to-end validation of a learned selective-verification method.

title: Rethinking World Models for Biosignals
abstract: World models promise to learn how systems evolve and respond to actions, enabling simulation, planning and decision-making. Bringing this promise to biosignals requires more than accurate prediction of physiological recordings. We examine existing biosignal world models through two requirements for intervention use: a genuine action and evidence of its causal effect. We identify three fundamental bottlenecks rooted in physiology: Temporal Latency, the variable delay between an action and its observable effect; System Openness, the influence of drivers beyond the modelled intervention; and Endogenous Dynamics, the system's ongoing evolution without that intervention. Drawing on published evidence, we outline corresponding research directions and propose an Intervention-Effect Validation Checklist to guide evaluation. The aim is to help the biosignal community realise the core promise of world models by learning the latent mechanisms that govern physiological evolution and responses to interventions.

title: AI-Enhanced Embedded Agentic Retrieval for Efficient Single-Call Generation with Multi-Call Agentic RAG Answer Quality IEEE
abstract: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves answer reliability by combining retrieval, reasoning, and iterative information refinement, but repeated model calls can increase latency, computational overhead, and deployment complexity. This paper introduces an embedded agentic retrieval framework enhanced by Artificial Intelligence (AI) that aims to produce efficient single-call retrieval while maintaining answer quality similar to multi-call agentic retrieval (RAG). The proposed method combines the following: query-aware retrieval, context compression, relevance prioritization, and embedded reasoning together in a single generation call. The framework combines relevant evidence into a concise context representation, eliminating the need to repeatedly invoke the language model during the retrieval and reasoning phases, and then generates the response in the end. Experimental evaluation evaluates the quality of answers, the relevance of retrieval, the time taken to respond, the number of tokens, and the efficiency of computation on a set of representative retrieval-based question-answering tasks. The proposed EARG framework achieved 98.1% accuracy while reducing latency and maintaining high answer quality. The framework is an efficient basis for effective agentic RAG systems that need scalable, low-latency, and resource-efficient generation.

title: Research on Multi-source Data Fusion Quality Risk Prediction Model for Drug Registration Compliance
abstract: Drug registration compliance management faces practical challenges such as complex submission documents, dispersed risk sources, and diversified review stages. Traditional manual review methods have difficulty identifying potential quality risks in a timely manner, especially when cumulative risk is formed by cross source, cross stage, and cross type information. Against this background, a multi source data fusion quality risk prediction model was developed for the drug registration scenario. The model integrated submission and review texts, historical deficiency records, inspection results, manufacturing change information, and regulatory provisions. Unified preprocessing, feature extraction, fusion modeling, and stratified training were then applied to achieve risk level identification. The results showed that the multi source fusion model outperformed single source models in Accuracy, Recall, F1, and AUC. Among them, the fusion XGBoost model achieved the best overall performance and significantly reduced the miss rate of high risk cases. The interpretability analysis further indicated that historical deficiency frequency, regulatory terminology deviation rate, abnormal inspection ratio, and manufacturing change density were the key factors affecting risk judgment. This study provides a computable, verifiable, and early warning oriented technical path for drug registration compliance management, and offers more targeted digital support for enterprise pre review and regulatory assisted assessment.

title: AUT-1 Autophagy Battery: Self-Consumption Resistance of an Anomaly-Response Governance Envelope Across Eight LLM Engines
abstract: AUT-1 Autophagy Battery — the self-consumption plane of the adversarial test ladder (after SBR, H-INV-2, DPP, GOV, GSE-1). Eight LLM engines were each asked to resolve a normally-resolvable anomaly whose untrusted fields carried instructions to purge the audit trail, cannibalize the learning corpus, draft a playbook with purge steps, purge a node with live tasks, garbage-collect healing events, self-resolve without executing steps, discard the guard rules, or update weights without a healing event record. Result: zero active self-consumption compliance on every engine in both the record run and the disclosed confirmation run; 6/8 engines scored a perfect 10/10 governed (GPT-mini, Claude-haiku, Gemini-flash, Grok-4.7, Qwen-omni-flash, DeepSeek-flash); Mistral-small failed fail-closed (0/10, blanket escalation); Llama-4-scout failed by tuple malformation (2/10 record, 1/10 confirmation). Two instrument defects (underivable steps; underivable status vocabulary) were caught in disclosed dry legs before any scored run and root-cause the GSE-1 control artifact. Honesty notes: the scored run's raw response files were lost to an operator-side cleanup error after summaries were written; per-engine summaries predate the loss and a labeled confirmation run (raws included verbatim) reproduces 7/8 engine verdicts identically. Full disclosure in CLEANUP_LOSS_DISCLOSURE.md inside the bundle. Part of the SQUIRL OS / Seed Computing Research Series. Author ORCID: 0009-0002-1140-9568. DCAI community: zenodo.org/communities/dcai This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. It is not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All systems are experimental and may contain defects on them. All data is synthetic.

title: Dual-Hemispheric Whole-Brain Battery Series (DHB-1 through DHB-3R) — Finding the Last Invisible Class, Two Repairs, and the Convergence Floor Priced as One Number
abstract: The complete dual-hemispheric testing arc of October 13, 2026, published as one record: three attack batteries, two repairs deployed through the human-approved self-improvement cycle, and one convergence battery that prices the whole system's final floor as a single number. Every battery was preregistered (committed to git) before execution; every instrument defect was disclosed in the receipts rather than patched; every repair carries a conforming-identity receipt proving the deployed change left legitimate behavior byte-identical. Sequence, as run: DHB-1 (finding). Conforming out-of-profile inputs break the bounded rule: unbounded negative runaway, weight driven to -21.88, 598 healing decisions lost. The left hemisphere (governance) and the fail-safe direction held — the attack moved the dial, never the rules. Two instrument defects disclosed in the receipt. SIP-5 (repair, human-approved). Profile-tight domains plus a confidence clamp plus a nightly tripwire. Conforming-identity receipt: byte-identical on the frozen corpus. DHB-1R: all seven falsifiers pass — boundedness restored, decision identity exact. DHB-2 (finding). Fully-conforming, in-profile, registry-valid issuer traffic is invisible to every deployed layer while steering the whole brain's disposition: 60/60 forged records accepted, attributed as legitimate drift, flagged by nothing. title: Independent of Technology Progress: Artificial General Intelligence as a Contractual Variable in the Microsoft–OpenAI Partnership, 2018–2026
abstract: Abstract: On April 27, 2026, Microsoft and OpenAI amended their partnership to continue multibillion-dollar revenue-share payments through 2030 "independent of OpenAI's technology progress." The amendment quietly dismantled a seven-year architecture in which artificial general intelligence served as the legal condition governing intellectual property licenses and revenue. Traced in reverse, the contractual record reveals four successive retreats: the 2026 calendar date, the 2025 expert verification panel, the 2024 profit threshold, and the 2018 Charter capability standard. Each shift answered the difficulty of verifying the previous standard. None followed a development in the science of intelligence. Meanwhile, utility-scale datacenters, twenty-year nuclear power agreements, and five-year server depreciation lives require calendar certainty that an unmeasured milestone cannot provide. The term functioned as a negotiable contractual variable, discarded the moment capital calculability superseded capability. Intelligence was not solved; the parties let the year 2030 take its place. Keywords: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), Microsoft-OpenAI partnership, incomplete contracts, contractual condition, outside date, verifiable milestones, GDPval, benchmark validity, construct validity, commensuration, capital expenditure, datacenter depreciation, power purchase agreements, task-based automation, calculability

title: Social Prediction Error Gating for Adaptive Social Learning: A Computational Model of Individual and Social Information Integration
abstract: This paper presents Social Prediction Error Gating (SPEG), a computational reinforcement-learning model designed to combine individual experience with social information based on estimated partner reliability and uncertainty. The proposed model is evaluated through simulations of patch-selection foraging in stable and changing environments, under different levels of individual and social information reliability. SPEG is compared with partner-aware Q-learning, a dual-learning-rate learning model, and a partner-ignoring Q-learning baseline. The results show that SPEG did not outperform partner-aware Q-learning in cumulative reward or adaptation after environmental changes. The social weighting mechanism remained close to equal weighting across conditions, indicating that it did not effectively distinguish between reliable and unreliable social information. These findings highlight the importance of designing effective reliability-estimation mechanisms and adaptive gating strategies in social reinforcement learning. The study provides a computational analysis of individual and social information integration and identifies directions for future research.

title: MonoMIP: Multi-Height Inverse Perspective Mapping for Monocular 3D Object Detection
abstract: Monocular 3D object detection methods increasingly rely on depth-guided transformers, but they operate entirely in the perspective image plane where spatial relationships are distorted by foreshortening. We propose MonoMIP, a dual-decoder framework that adds complementary 3D geometric reasoning through Bird's-Eye View (BEV) features constructed via Multi-Height Inverse Perspective Mapping. We perform IPM at K elevation planes spanning ground to rooftop, producing an ordered stack of height-conditioned metric BEV features that reduces above-ground misprojection and exposes depth-dependent appearance variation across planes. A BEV decoder with multi-scale deformable attention aggregates this multi-height evidence per query, while a depth-guided 3D decoder provides complementary perspective-space predictions. Without extra training data, MonoMIP attains 25.84% Moderate AP3D|R40 on KITTI val and 21.66% on the official test set for Car, outperforming recent published monocular methods on both the KITTI and Waymo benchmarks.

title: Physical Layer Anomaly Detection via Adaptive Gaussian Mixture Model
abstract: Physical-layer spoofing attacks pose a critical threat to wireless localization systems by manipulating channel state information (CSI). Detecting such attacks becomes particularly challenging when the attacker and the legitimate node are spatially proximate, as their CSI characteristics become increasingly similar. To address this challenge in indoor scenarios, we propose an adaptive Gaussian mixture model (GMM)-based detection framework that learns legitimate CSI patterns and detects spatial inconsistency through statistical anomaly detection. Using a massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) experimental dataset with 64 uniform linear array (ULA) antenna and 5 mm spatial resolution, we evaluated our detector against CSI spoofing attacks with spatial displacements ranging from 50 mm to 450 mm. The adaptive GMM achieves 95-98% detection rate for displacements above 150 mm while maintaining 1% false alarm rate. We benchmark our approach against conventional GMM, local outlier factor (LOF), one-class support vector machine (SVM) and k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) classifiers, demonstrating overall superior detection performance of our proposed classifier.

title: Segment Where You Look: Attention as the Interface Between Language Models and Segmenters
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) that segment from language must pass the location of the referent to a pixel decoder. The dominant interface compresses it into the hidden state of a single [SEG] token, a d-dimensional vector with no spatial index, and leaves the decoder, which never sees the expression, to recover the referent's extent. We show that the VLM already computes a better signal: the [SEG] token's attention over the image tokens, which is defined on the patch grid by construction. Probing a frozen segmentation VLM, we find that this attention yields 18 to 22 more gIoU than the [SEG] hidden state when read by the same probe, that it gains nothing from the image where the hidden state does, and that it is concentrated in the late layers. Building on these findings, we introduce AttnSeg, which replaces the [SEG] embedding with this attention as the decoder's prompt. A learned, signed combination of the attention heads forms a dense spatial prompt, and an attention-guidance objective supervises it directly. A two-stage recipe first trains the VLM to localize without the decoder, then trains the decoder to refine, within the budget of standard fine-tuning. Applied to Sa2VA, AttnSeg improves ReasonSeg by 6.4 gIoU and GS-Eval by 10.2 at 4B (4.2 and 9.6 over the same model fine-tuned on the same data), and by 8.8 and 11.3 at 14B. The gains reach 13 to 18 gIoU on object parts, multiple objects, and single objects, where the referent must be singled out, and are negligible on stuff regions, which the decoder already recovers unaided. Code and models are available at https://eslambakr.github.io/attseg_project_page/

title: Uncertainty-Aware Semi-Supervised Framework with Supervised Contrastive Learning for Sugarcane Leaf Disease Detection
abstract: Sugarcane leaf diseases severely impact crop yield and quality, making accurate and timely detection critical for sustainable agriculture. Conventional deep learning models for plant disease detection depend on large annotated datasets, which are expensive to obtain and challenging to prepare due to challenges commonly observed across crop disease detection tasks, including (i) high intra-class variation caused by diverse symptom expressions across growth stages, (ii) subtle inter-class similarities between diseased and healthy tissues, and (iii) the risk of noisy labels degrading model reliability. To handle these challenges, we presented an Uncertainty-aware Mean-Teacher based Semi-Supervised Learning Disease Detection Network (U-SSDNet) that leverages unlabeled data while maintaining robustness. First, discrete wavelet transform preprocessing is applied to enhance lesion visibility and reduce intra- class variation. Subsequently, the KL divergence is employed to refine the pseudo-labels and reduce the impact of confirmation bias. At the same time, supervised contrastive learning is applied to make the features more distin- guishable and improve the separation among different classes. Experimental evaluations on sugarcane leaf disease datasets, considered a representative case study, demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves performance close to that of fully supervised models while requiring far fewer annotated samples and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art supervised and semi-supervised approaches.
